item.passage:
The weigh-off at the Halden County Fair started at nine, but by eight the line of trailers already stretched back past the poultry barn. Rosa sat on the fender of her grandfather's trailer and watched the forklift raise each pumpkin, pallet and all, onto the platform scale at the front of the line.

Their pumpkin had a name painted on its side, as most pumpkins in the line did. Rosa had lettered CORNELIA there in June. Since then she had watered it every evening, buried its vines at the joints so they would root along their length, and measured it each Sunday with a cloth tape: once around the middle, once over the top from stem to blossom end, once from side to side. Her grandfather added the three numbers and looked up the total on a chart taped inside the shed door, which turned inches into a guess at pounds. On the last Sunday the chart had said 581.

The pumpkins ahead of them were enormous. Mrs. Lisk's, which went up just before theirs, was so wide that the forklift driver climbed down twice to check his clearance. The board read 1,012 pounds. The crowd along the rope clapped the way people clap for something they expected, and Rosa clapped with them.

Then Cornelia went up. The numbers on the board flickered and settled at 634.

"Fifty-three over the tape," her grandfather said. "She went heavy."

Cornelia finished fifth out of twenty-two. The ribbons went to the top three, and Rosa watched Mrs. Lisk pin a blue one to the pallet beside her pumpkin while a man from the newspaper took her picture.

Afterward the growers began cutting their pumpkins open at the back of the lot to save the seeds. Rosa's grandfather scooped out a handful of Cornelia's, rinsed them under the spigot, dropped them into a paper envelope, and walked straight over to Mrs. Lisk. He asked whether she would trade a dozen of hers for a dozen of these. Rosa stayed by the trailer, her ears hot, and studied the gravel so that no one would see her face. It seemed to her like losing a race and then asking the winner for her shoes.

Mrs. Lisk laughed. "I was about to come and ask you," she said. "Anyone can grow big from big seed. A pumpkin that beats the tape by fifty pounds has thick walls, and thick walls are the thing I can't seem to get." She wrote 634 ORTEGA on his envelope in marker, tucked it into her jacket, and handed him one of her own.

On the drive home Rosa held Mrs. Lisk's envelope on her lap. Her grandfather said that next year's pumpkin was already in there. Rosa thought of the other envelope, the one with 634 written on it, riding home in Mrs. Lisk's jacket. She had spent the whole afternoon thinking about fifth place, and she had not once thought of 634 as a number anyone would want to write down.

My grandmother's binoculars lived on the sill of her kitchen window, in a leather case so old that its strap had been replaced with a length of red shoelace. They were heavy and black and dented on one corner, and they had belonged to her father, who carried them on fishing boats out of a northern port I have never seen.

Everyone in my family used them the same way. You raised them to your face, shut your left eye, and looked through the right barrel only. My mother did it, my uncle did it, and my grandmother had done it for fifty years at that window above the harbor. When I asked why, she said the left side "went funny" if you tried to use both. I tried both. The harbor slid apart into two harbors, one floating a little above the other, and my eyes ached for an hour.

So I learned the family way. For three summers, staying with her, I watched ferries, hawks, and the neighbor's cat through one barrel with the other eye squeezed shut, and I thought of the binoculars as a kind of telescope that happened to come in a pair.

The summer I was fifteen, I carried them to a camera shop downtown with my birthday money in my pocket. The repairman, a tall man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, looked through them for about two seconds. "Somebody dropped these," he said. "The prisms inside have shifted, so each side is pointing at a slightly different spot." He could realign them, he said, for forty dollars, by Thursday.

On Thursday he handed them back across the counter and told me to look out the front window with both eyes. I did, and the street jumped toward me. The parked cars stood out from the buildings behind them, and a lamppost was plainly closer than the bus shelter beyond it. Through one barrel the world had always looked like a photograph. Through both it had depth, and I stood in the shop for several minutes moving from one thing to the next.

That evening I set the binoculars back in my grandmother's hands at the kitchen window and told her to keep both eyes open. She raised them toward the harbor, and then, without seeming to notice, she shut her left eye.

I almost said something. Instead I watched her follow a fishing boat out past the breakwater, one eye closed, her face as calm as it always was at that window. It occurred to me that the binoculars had been broken for all the years she had used them, and that for her they had never been broken at all.

Until 1874, a fire in the river town of Callow Bend was announced the way any emergency was: someone ran to the Methodist church and rang its bell as fast as the rope would allow. The bell brought the volunteer fire company out of their houses quickly enough. It did not tell them where to go. Men gathered in the square, asked whoever was there, and set off, and on more than one night the company split in two and hauled its equipment toward opposite ends of town.

In the spring of 1874 the company's captain, a harness maker named Jonas Weller, put a plan before the town council. Callow Bend would be divided into five wards, each with a number. When a fire was reported, the ringer would strike the ward's number, pause, and strike it again for as long as the company took to assemble: three strokes, a pause, three strokes for a fire in the third ward. The council approved the plan in April, ordered five hundred printed cards showing a map of the wards, and paid a boy fifty cents to deliver one to every house.

Within a month the company was reaching fires in about half the time. So was everyone else. The ward number told every household at once where the excitement was, and on summer evenings especially, sightseers and boys reached a fire ahead of the hand engine and filled the lane in front of it. Weller called them "the parade" and complained of them at every meeting. At a fire on Tanner Street that July, the engine was held up for several minutes while men shoved a path through the crowd, and a barn burned to the ground that Weller believed could have been saved.

Several council members proposed going back to the old way of ringing. A bell that told everyone where to go, one of them argued, was a bell that sent everyone. Weller surprised the council by arguing against them. The crowd was a problem, he said, only as long as it stood and watched. The company's engine was pumped by long handles called brakes, worked by as many as eight men on each side, and the company's own members tired within a quarter of an hour. The parade had arms.

At his urging the council passed an ordinance that August. The captain could call any able-bodied man present at a fire to the brakes or the bucket line, and a man who refused could be fined a dollar. Two members of the company were to run ahead of the engine with a rope to clear the lane, and boys under fourteen were to be sent home.

The council's minutes for the next several years mention the parade less and less. Crowds still came. Turn over a stone in a clean, cold stream, and you may find what looks like a short twig or a tube of sand crawling slowly across it. Inside is the larva of a caddisfly, an insect closely related to moths and butterflies. Caddisflies spend most of their lives as larvae, and the larvae of nearly all species live in fresh water. Many of them build portable cases around their soft bodies, binding the pieces together with silk from glands near the mouth.

The materials vary with the species. Some larvae fit grains of sand into a smooth, slightly curved tube; others use small pebbles, bits of leaf cut to size, short lengths of stem, or the empty shells of tiny snails. Many species build in so consistent a style that a specialist can often tell which group a larva belongs to from its case alone. A larva enlarges its case by adding material at the front, the end its head and legs reach out of, so the oldest part of a case is at the back.

The case seems to do several jobs at once. It shields the larva's soft abdomen from small predators, and a case of sand or leaf bits blends into the stream bed. It also helps the larva breathe. A caddisfly larva takes in oxygen from the water through its skin and, in many species, through thin gills on its abdomen; by rippling its body inside the case, it keeps fresh water flowing through the tube. In fast water, a heavy case of stones may also help a larva stay on the bottom instead of being swept downstream.

Not every caddisfly larva carries a home. Some species build fixed shelters, called retreats, attached to rocks in the current, and spin silk nets beside them that catch drifting bits of food. Others roam freely over the stones, hunting smaller animals, until it is time to pupate.

Case builders are also choosy. In laboratory studies, larvae whose cases have been gently removed will usually build new ones, and they appear to handle particles with their legs and mouthparts before using them, passing over grains that are too large or the wrong shape. When people have offered larvae unusual materials, such as flakes of gold or chips of gemstone, many have built with them, producing cases that no stream could supply.

Caddisfly larvae also matter beyond their own streams. Along with the young of mayflies and stoneflies, many kinds are sensitive to pollution and to low oxygen, so biologists who survey streams often treat them as a sign of water quality: a stream that supports many kinds of caddisflies is usually in good condition. At the end of the larval stage, a case-building larva fastens its case to a stone, seals it, and pupates inside. The adult that emerges looks rather like a small, dull moth, with wings covered in fine hairs, which is where the group's scientific name, Trichoptera, meaning "hairy wings," comes from.

The case seems to do several jobs at once. It shields the larva's soft abdomen from small predators, and a case of sand or leaf bits blends into the stream bed. It also helps the larva breathe. A caddisfly larva takes in oxygen from the water through its skin and, in many species, through thin gills on its abdomen; by rippling its body inside the case, it keeps fresh water flowing through the tube. In fast water, a heavy case of stones may also help a larva stay on the bottom instead of being swept downstream.

Not every caddisfly larva carries a home. Some species build fixed shelters, called retreats, attached to rocks in the current, and spin silk nets beside them that catch drifting bits of food. Others roam freely over the stones, hunting smaller animals, until it is time to pupate.

Case builders are also choosy. In laboratory studies, larvae whose cases have been gently removed will usually build new ones, and they appear to handle particles with their legs and mouthparts before using them, passing over grains that are too large or the wrong shape. When people have offered larvae unusual materials, such as flakes of gold or chips of gemstone, many have built with them, producing cases that no stream could supply.

Caddisfly larvae also matter beyond their own streams. Along with the young of mayflies and stoneflies, many kinds are sensitive to pollution and to low oxygen, so biologists who survey streams often treat them as a sign of water quality: a stream that supports many kinds of caddisflies is usually in good condition. At the end of the larval stage, a case-building larva fastens its case to a stone, seals it, and pupates inside. The adult that emerges looks rather like a small, dull moth, with wings covered in fine hairs, which is where the group's scientific name, Trichoptera, meaning "hairy wings," comes from.
